title: Why gravity ruins large colloidal crystals
question: At what particle size does sedimentation beat Brownian self-assembly, on the ground and in orbit?

headline.text: On the ground, silica spheres larger than about 1.1 um sink faster than Brownian motion can arrange them (Pe > 1). At an ISS-like 1e-6 g that limit moves to about 36 um, and at 1e-7 g to about 63 um. Physics computation, not a measurement.

evidence_note: physics computation from textbook formulas (Stokes drag, Peclet number); no data were measured

datasets.name: Physical constants and fluid properties
datasets.notes: kB exact (SI 2019); water at 25 C: density 997.05 kg/m3, viscosity 0.890 mPa s (standard reference values, e.g. CRC Handbook). Particle densities: Stober silica ~2.0 g/cm3 (fused silica is 2.2), PMMA 1.19, polystyrene 1.05 g/cm3.

datasets.name: ISS quasi-steady acceleration level
datasets.notes: ISS design requirement of about 1 micro-g at payload locations; PIMS reports measured quasi-steady levels typically a few micro-g (<= ~5 ug). See also NASA NTRS 20100042410 (Assembly Complete microgravity verification).

datasets.name: OpenAlex works (random sample, seed 42)
datasets.notes: title_and_abstract.search: "colloidal crystal" OR "colloidal crystals" OR "colloidal photonic crystal" OR "artificial opal" OR "inverse opal"; type article; has abstract.

compute.where: local (stdlib Python; physics < 1 s; OpenAlex sample 20 API pages)

method: Hard spheres of diameter 100 nm to 5 um (120 log-spaced sizes) in water at 25 C.

Stokes velocity v = 2 a^2 drho g / (9 eta); Peclet number Pe = (4/3) pi a^4 drho g / kT (equivalently v a / D with D = kT / (6 pi eta a)); gravitational length l_g = a / Pe; time to sink 1 mm = 1 mm / v.
Three gravity levels: 1 g; 1e-6 g (ISS quasi-steady design level); 1e-7 g (free-flyer drag level, a placeholder until the orbit workstream measures it).
Crossover diameter where Pe = 1: d* = 2 (3 kT / (4 pi drho g))^(1/4), so d* scales as g^(-1/4).

charts.title: On the ground, gravity beats Brownian motion above about 1 um
charts.subtitle: Gravitational Peclet number Pe = (4/3) pi a^4 drho g / kT, spheres in water, 25 C, 1 g
charts.caption: Physics computation, not a measurement. Pe < 1 means thermal motion can still rearrange particles faster than they settle by one radius. It does not by itself guarantee a good crystal: polydispersity, interactions and drying also matter.

charts.title: Silica spheres: Peclet number at 1 g, ISS level and free-flyer level
charts.subtitle: Pe scales linearly with g, so the Pe = 1 crossover diameter scales as g^(-1/4)
charts.caption: Physics computation. The 1e-7 g level is a placeholder until the orbit workstream measures the free-flyer drag acceleration from tracking data. ISS measured quasi-steady levels are typically a few micro-g, not exactly 1e-6 g.

charts.title: Time for silica spheres to sink 1 mm
charts.subtitle: Stokes velocity v = 2 a^2 drho g / (9 eta); t = 1 mm / v
charts.caption: Physics computation for a single sphere in an unbounded fluid (dilute limit). Real concentrated suspensions settle more slowly (hindered settling, roughly (1-phi)^5), so these times are lower bounds for dense samples.

charts.title: Gravitational length vs sample height (silica)
charts.subtitle: l_g = kT / (m_b g): the height over which the equilibrium concentration falls by e
charts.caption: Physics computation. A sample much taller than l_g ends up as a dense sediment with a concentration gradient, which compresses and strains crystals. On the ground, l_g of 300 nm silica is ~0.03 mm, far below a 1 cm sample; at 1e-6 g it is ~30 m.

charts.title: Largest sphere diameter that Brownian motion can still organise (Pe = 1)
charts.subtitle: Crossover diameter d* = 2 (3 kT / (4 pi drho g))^(1/4)
charts.caption: Physics computation. Below d* thermal motion dominates; above it, settling does. The 1e-7 g row uses a placeholder acceleration.

charts.subtitle: Sphere diameters stated in 135 of 4,000 randomly sampled OpenAlex abstracts (one median value per paper)
charts.caption: This chart alone is our computation on public data (OpenAlex abstracts, regex extraction), not physics. Bin edges at the 1 g crossover diameters of silica and polystyrene. Only ~3% of abstracts state a sphere size, so this is a small, abstract-only sample.

findings: At 1 g the Pe = 1 crossover is at d* = 1.12 um for silica, 1.70 um for PMMA and 2.35 um for polystyrene (density-matched particles settle less).
At 1e-6 g the silica crossover moves to 35.6 um and at 1e-7 g to 63.2 um, so every size from 100 nm to 5 um has Pe < 1 in orbit.
300 nm silica spheres, the size used for visible-light photonic crystals, sink 1 mm in 5.03 hours on the ground and in 573 years at 1e-6 g.

For visible-range spheres (~200-300 nm) Pe is already below 1 on the ground, so the gravity problem for them is not single-particle settling but the dense sediment: the gravitational length (30 um for 300 nm silica) is far smaller than a mm-cm sample, giving concentration gradients and self-compression. Larger (IR, 1-5 um) spheres have Pe >> 1 on the ground.
Published context (not our result): hard-sphere colloids that stayed glassy on Earth crystallised in microgravity on Space Shuttle STS-73 (Zhu et al., Nature 387, 883, 1997).

Literature sample (our computation on OpenAlex abstracts): of 135 papers that state a sphere size, the median is 335 nm and 8 (5.9%) use spheres above silica's 1 g crossover of 1.1 um. Most experiments sit in the sub-micron range that visible-light photonics needs, where Pe < 1 even on the ground; the gravity-limited regime (> ~1 um, infrared photonics, large-sphere model systems) is the under-explored part. Why authors choose sizes is not in the data.
limitations: Physics computation, not a measurement or simulation of crystal growth.
Dilute single-sphere Stokes settling; dense suspensions settle more slowly (hindered settling), and walls, convection, charge and polydispersity are ignored.
Pe < 1 is a necessary condition for gravity not to dominate, not a sufficient condition for a large defect-free crystal.
1e-7 g is a placeholder; the real free-flyer level comes from the orbit workstream. ISS measured quasi-steady levels are typically a few micro-g (d* then shrinks by ~5^(1/4) = 1.5x).
Particle densities are typical values; Stober silica density varies (~1.9-2.2 g/cm3).

Literature sizes: abstract-only regex extraction from a seeded random sample of OpenAlex works; only papers that state a size in the abstract are counted, a few matches may be pore or film sizes rather than sphere diameters, and the sample was run from a laptop because OpenAlex's anonymous budget is per IP.
future_big_data: Mine the literature (e.g. OpenAlex/Crossref full text) for particle diameters, materials and crystal sizes reported in colloidal photonic-crystal papers, and place them on these curves.
Use the measured free-flyer acceleration spectrum (orbit workstream) instead of the 1e-7 g placeholder, including its time variation.
Pair with Brownian-dynamics simulations of sedimenting crystallisation at each g level.
